blocks.text: A button triggers an immediate action, such as submit, confirm, open or delete.
On this page:   Live demo   ·   Overview   ·   Formatting   ·   Content   ·   Behaviors

Preview of the default variant (Variant=Primary, Size=Sm, State=Default, Radius=Default) in the light and dark modes of semantic.color. This is a static preview — no interactive source (Storybook or prototype) is linked yet.
No accessibility test records exist for this component yet. Automated contrast results are on the Accessibility tab.

A button triggers an immediate action in the current context — submitting a form, confirming a choice, opening something or deleting an item. Four emphasis levels (Primary, Secondary, Ghost, Danger) keep the most important action on a screen the easiest one to find.
Use buttons for actions only. If activating it takes the user to another page or location, it is navigation and must not be a button.
•   To let users submit, confirm, open or delete something immediately.
•   To mark the single most important action in a context — Primary.
•   To offer supporting actions of lower weight next to a primary one — Secondary or Ghost.
•   To trigger destructive or irreversible actions such as delete or remove — Danger.
•   When the action navigates to another page or location — use a text link instead.
•   Don't use Danger styling for actions that aren't destructive — use Primary, Secondary or Ghost.
•   ① Container — the interactive wrapper; owns variant, size and state.
•   ② Icon (optional) — leading or trailing, never both. Vertically centred with the label. Decorative icons are hidden from assistive technology.
•   ③ Label — text describing the action. Required unless the button is icon-only.
Not shown: the loading indicator that replaces the leading slot while is-loading is on. It is not built yet.
Dense UIs, toolbars and table rows.
The default size for most buttons.
Primary page calls to action and touch-first screens.
Every variant shares the same size scale. Each size defines its own height, horizontal padding, font size and icon size.
Content is always centred horizontally and vertically. The icon sits on the side set by the icon property and is vertically centred with the label; the icon–label gap is the same across variants.
Label hidden with Show label = off. Must have an accessible label (aria-label).

Buttons hug their content within the size's padding and are not stretched. A full-width option (container spans its parent, content stays centred) is defined in the component skill but not exposed as a Figma property yet.
Use one primary action, paired with lower-emphasis actions.
Don't place two primary buttons in the same context — they read as equally important.
Keep every button in a group the same size.
Don't mix sizes in one group.
Use Danger only for destructive or irreversible actions.
Don't use Danger styling for a non-destructive action.
•   Use a verb that describes the action, e.g. Save, Delete, Open.
•   Required on every button unless it is icon-only.
•   Optional — leading or trailing, never both.
•   Decorative icons must be hidden from assistive technology.
•   Icon-only buttons must have an accessible label (aria-label).
A button has no persistent on/off state: it runs its action and returns to rest. Every variant starts in the Default state.
•   Hover — the pointer is over the button.
•   Pressed — during a press; gives immediate visual feedback so the press registers.
•   Focused — keyboard focus; always shows a visible focus indicator.
•   Loading — action in progress. Defined in the skill but not built yet.
See the Style tab for how each state looks.
Clicking anywhere on the button runs its action. Disabled buttons ignore clicks. While a button is loading, repeat clicks are ignored until the action finishes.
Full keyboard details are on the Accessibility tab.
While is-loading is on, a spinner replaces the leading slot and the label may stay for width stability. The button blocks repeat activation until the action resolves.

•   To list actions or destinations in a menu — Menu.

•   To show a setting with a short description — Setting.

A badge is a small element that communicates a status, a count, a label or a notification on another element.
On this page:   Live demo   ·   Overview   ·   Formatting   ·   Content   ·   Behaviors   ·   Related

Preview of the default variant (Status=Success, Style=Filled, Type=Text, Size=Sm) in the light and dark modes of semantic.color. Static preview — no interactive source (Storybook or prototype) is linked yet.
No accessibility test records exist for this component yet. Automated contrast results are on the Accessibility tab.
A badge annotates another element with a status, a count or a short label. It never stands alone as a primary control.
Each status color maps to exactly one meaning and is never reused for another.
•   To show the status of an item — success, warning, error, info or neutral.
•   To show a count, such as unread notifications — Numeric.
•   To show that something needs attention without a count — Dot.
•   To tag an item with a short label — Text; a dismissible badge lets users remove it.
•   As a primary action, button or main navigation target — use a Button.
•   For more than a short label, a single count or one icon — no paragraphs, multiple icons or nested badges.
•   ① Container — the pill-shaped container that wraps all content.
•   ② Icon (optional) — leading and vertically centred with the label; text badges only.
•   ③ Label — text or a number; omitted on dot badges.
•   ④ Dismiss (optional) — trailing close control, shown only when the badge is dismissible; text badges only.
Height is fixed per size; horizontal padding scales with size.
Content is centred in the container. The icon is always leading and vertically centred with the label, with a fixed gap (space/inline/xs).
Place a badge next to or on the element it describes. Content must never overflow, break or expand the parent layout.
Use one style for badges of the same status in a view.
Don't mix styles within the same status group.
Don't render a wider raw count.
Use a status color only for its meaning.
Don't reuse a status color for an unrelated meaning.
•   A short label or a single count — nothing longer.
•   If the count is above max-count (default 99), show {max-count}+.
•   A count of 0 doesn't render unless explicitly forced.
•   Dot badges ignore the count and label.
Text badges truncate with an ellipsis at their maximum width and never wrap to a second line.
Badges are static by default and have no hover, focus or disabled states. Only a clickable badge defines Hover, Focus (visible focus ring) and Disabled.
A clickable badge exposes one clear action. A dismissible badge's close control is separately focusable and emits a dismiss event.
Moves focus to the dismiss control (dismissible badges only)
Full keyboard details are on the Accessibility tab.
•   Button — use for actions; a badge must never act as a primary action.

No accessibility test records exist for this component yet. Automated contrast results are on the Accessibility tab.
An accordion condenses long content into scannable headers. Users reveal one or more panels on demand — which also means content stays hidden until they open it.
Only one panel open at a time; opening one closes the others.
Any number of panels open independently.
Items separated only by spacing; no outline.
Single- vs multiple-expand is behavior (expandMode), not a Figma variant. Bordered and Borderless are the Style variant.
•   To condense long content into scannable headers that users open on demand.
•   For FAQ-style content, where users pick the questions they need.
•   For content users must read in full.
•   ① Header — a heading element wrapping the trigger button; the whole row is the hit target.
•   ② Title — start-aligned label for the section.
•   ③ Icon — chevron showing collapsed or expanded; decorative.
•   ④ Content panel — revealed on expand.
The title is start-aligned and the icon end-aligned on the same row. The trigger spans the full header width.

Items stack vertically at full width — never side by side. Spacing between items is consistent; borderless accordions rely on it as their only separator. Avoid nesting accordions; if you must, indent and limit to one level.
In single-expand mode, keep one panel open at a time.
Don't allow two panels expanded at once in single-expand mode.
•   Wrapped in a heading (h2–h4) that fits the page outline.
•   Padding is tighter for text and roomier for complex content (contentType).
•   Every collapsed panel shows its icon, so hidden content always has a visible cue.
Items start collapsed (Default). Activating the trigger toggles its own panel; in single-expand mode, opening a panel collapses the one that was open.
•   Focused — 3px focus ring on the header; never suppressed.
•   Disabled — dimmed, can't change state, skipped in tab order.
See the Style tab for how each state looks.
Clicking anywhere in the header toggles the panel.

Always pair autoplay with a visible, reachable pause control.
Don't autoplay without a pause control.
Don't hide navigation with no alternative way to advance.
Give users a way to advance — controls, pagination or swipe.

•   Off-screen slides are inert — not reachable by Tab.
•   Dots show position and count; the active dot is larger.

•   Loading — placeholders for slides that haven't loaded yet.

On this page:   Live demo   ·   Overview   ·   Formatting   ·   Content   ·   Behaviors   ·   Related

A dialog interrupts the page to focus the user on exactly one task or decision. It's the most disruptive surface available — it blocks everything else until it's resolved — so use it sparingly.
Embedded form fields; the only type with an Error state.
A full-height panel (800px tall) in three widths.
Information to be aware of; no decision
An action is needed to complete and close
The user must actively acknowledge something
Cancel + Previous + Next (or the completing action on the last step)
•   To get an immediate response needed to continue something the user just started.
•   To notify the user of urgent information tied to their current work.
•   To confirm a decision — especially a destructive or irreversible one.
•   For information that isn't urgent — use an inline Alert instead.
•   For tasks users repeat often — let them complete it on the page.
•   When even the largest size isn't enough room — use a full page.
•   ① Title — a short, specific verb phrase naming the task.
•   ② Subtitle (optional) — short context below the title (Has subtitle).
•   ③ Close icon — always available for dismissal.
•   ④ Body — message text and/or embedded content such as form fields.
•   ⑤ Secondary action — e.g. Cancel, on the left.
•   ⑥ Primary action — the one action that completes the task, on the right.
Not shown: the overlay — the dimmed layer behind the dialog. It isn't built as a component yet.
Choose the size by content: brief text fits Small; complex embedded content needs Medium or Large. If content keeps scrolling, move up a size; if the largest isn't enough, use a full page.
Right-aligned, about half the footer width
Secondary left, primary right, each about half, flush to the edges
Each about a quarter, clustered right; only the rightmost may be primary
Cancel (ghost) alone on the left; Previous (secondary) and Next (primary) on the right

Center the dialog vertically for short, predictable content, or pin it at a fixed offset from the top for longer or variable content. Use a dimmed backdrop by default. Clicking the backdrop may close passive dialogs, but never transactional or destructive ones. Avoid opening a dialog from inside another dialog.
Secondary (Cancel) on the left, primary on the right — one clear emphasis.
Don't use two primary buttons — the user can't tell which action is safe.
For destructive actions, name the action in the title and use a danger-styled, specific button.
Don't use vague titles or buttons like OK for a destructive action.
•   A short, specific verb phrase that matches whatever opened the dialog.
•   For a very short message, let the title carry it and skip the body.
•   Only when the purpose isn't obvious from the title.
•   Brief — only the fields and content needed to complete the task.
•   Short, specific verbs — Delete, Save, Add — not vague labels like Done.
•   OK is fine only for the acknowledgment pattern.
When the body needs to scroll, the header and footer stay fixed and only the body scrolls, with a fade at the bottom edge. Content never scrolls horizontally — move up a size instead.
•   Loading — the footer buttons are disabled while the action runs, preventing a double submit.
•   Error — Form only: an error banner at the top of the body, with the fields to correct.
See the Style tab for how each state looks.
•   Opens only as the direct result of a user action — never unprompted.
•   Initial focus lands on the first form field, or on the primary button if there's no form.

•   Close with the close icon, Escape, or — for passive dialogs only — a click outside. Cancel reverts any staged changes.
